99.title: The child on the leaf
99.hook: a sage is breathed in and out by a child on a banyan leaf; why Hindus see time as cycles that rest in God
99.carry: time breathes in cycles, and rests in god
99.tomorrow: why is half of Shiva a woman?
99.howItsDone: Hindu teaching pictures time in great cycles of creation and dissolution, with the world resting in God between them; images of the child on the banyan leaf recall Markandeya's vision. In yoga, kumbhaka, gentle breath retention, is taught gradually by a teacher.

screen: `DAY NINETY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arjuna's restless mind, and the out-breath: four counts in, six counts out. Your line was Arjuna's wind: the mind follows the breath. Today, a sage who gets breathed in by a god, and the pause at the top of every breath.
screen: `ARJUNA'S WIND: THE MIND FOLLOWS THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: The world has ended. Not in fire: in water. A sage named Markandeya is swimming alone in a dark ocean with no shore, for what feels like ages. Then, on the water, a banyan tree, and on one of its leaves, a baby. Glowing, calm, sucking his own toe. Markandeya swims closer. The baby breathes in, and the sage is pulled into his body like a mosquito on the wind.
screen: `THE WORLD UNDER WATER.` → `A BABY ON A BANYAN LEAF.` → `BREATHED IN LIKE A MOSQUITO.`

segments.voice: Inside the child, Markandeya finds everything. Mountains, rivers, cities, even his own little hermitage. The whole world, alive inside one small body. Then the baby breathes out, and the sage tumbles back into the dark water, and there's the child again on the leaf, smiling. This is from the Bhagavata Purana, and the child is Vishnu. Here's the teaching under it, one of Hinduism's biggest ideas: time moves in cycles. The world isn't made once and finished. It comes out, lives, dissolves, and rests in God, and then comes out again, age after age. Between worlds, it's often pictured as Vishnu resting on the great ocean. Nothing is lost there; everything is held, waiting for the next breath. Now the word. Kumbhaka, from kumbha, a clay water jar: the breath resting still, like water in a jar. Every breath has two small pauses, one at the top after the in-breath, and one at the bottom after the out-breath. Some teachers like to read them as tiny echoes of that great rest. Keep it gentle: two soft counts, no clamping the throat. The old yoga texts describe long holds, but those were taught one to one, by a teacher watching closely. If a pause makes you anxious or short of air, skip it. If you're pregnant, or have high blood pressure, or a heart or lung condition, leave the holds out and just notice where the pauses would be. For Hindus, a stop isn't the end of the story. It's the world resting in God before the next breath.
screen: `THE WHOLE WORLD INSIDE HIM.` · `TIME MOVES IN CYCLES.` · `BETWEEN WORLDS, IT RESTS IN GOD.` · `KUMBHA — A WATER JAR.` · `TWO SOFT COUNTS, NEVER A STRAIN.` · then, large: `TIME BREATHES IN CYCLES, AND RESTS IN GOD.`

segments.voice: Breathe in for four and rest at the top for two, then breathe out for six and rest at the bottom for two, and let the next breath come. If the holds feel easy, keep them; if not, just notice where the top and bottom are without stopping, and either way is the practice. Look for the still point, like the child resting on the leaf.
Kumbhaka. From kumbha, a water jar. The pause in the breath, where everything rests for a moment.
screen: `KUMBHAKA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Hold on to it: time breathes in cycles, and rests in God. Markandeya was breathed out to see it. Day ninety-nine, in the books.

100.title: Half Shiva, half Shakti
100.hook: a devotee tries to honor Shiva without Parvati; why Hindus worship God as Ardhanarishvara, both halves at once
100.carry: shiva and shakti can't be split
100.tomorrow: the Goddess once came as a swarm of bees. why bees?
100.howItsDone: Ardhanarishvara, Shiva and Parvati as one figure, is worshipped and carved in temples across India. In yoga practice, nadi shodhana, alternate-nostril breathing using the thumb and ring finger of the right hand, is a common daily pranayama, often done before meditation or puja.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Markandeya, breathed in and out by the child on the leaf. Your line was time breathes in cycles, and rests in God. Today is day one hundred, and the breath goes one side at a time.
screen: `TIME BREATHES IN CYCLES, AND RESTS IN GOD.`

segments.voice: Day one hundred, and a story about a devotee who went too far. Bhringi loved Shiva so much that he would walk circles around him in worship, the way people still walk around a shrine. Only Shiva. Never Parvati, sitting right beside him. So she moved closer, until there was no gap. Bhringi tried to squeeze between them anyway. And in the telling, Parvati did something remarkable: she merged into Shiva's body. Now there was one figure. The right half Shiva, the left half Parvati. No gap left to slip through.
screen: `HE CIRCLED ONLY SHIVA.` → `SHE MOVED CLOSER.` → `ONE BODY: HALF SHIVA, HALF PARVATI.`

segments.voice: That form has a name: Ardhanarishvara, the Lord who is half woman. It's carved in temples across India, and has been for many centuries. Bhringi learned the hard way. In many tellings, Parvati took back what a mother gives, his flesh and blood, and he couldn't stand, until Shiva, kind even then, gave him a third leg. Temples often show him beside Shiva, thin as bone, on three legs. And here's the teaching, one of Hinduism's biggest: Shiva and Shakti. Shiva is often described as pure awareness, perfectly still. Shakti, the Goddess, is power, the energy that moves everything. Many Hindus say you never have one without the other: Shiva without Shakti can't move, and power without awareness has nothing to stand on. To honor God is to honor both. Now the breath. Nadi shodhana: nadi, a channel, and shodhana, clearing. Yoga pictures two main channels: ida on the left, cool like the moon, and pingala on the right, warm like the sun, with sushumna in the center, along the spine. Breathing side to side, the old teachers said, brings them into balance, and many teachers read yoga's aim as the two meeting in the middle, Shakti rising to meet Shiva. Here's how. Right hand up, index and middle fingers folded. Thumb closes the right nostril; breathe in through the left. Ring finger closes the left, open the right; breathe out through the right. In through the right, switch, out through the left. Gentle, slow, no holding. If your nose is blocked, skip it and picture the breath moving side to side. If you get lightheaded, stop.

segments.voice: Right hand up, index and middle fingers folded: thumb closes the right side, breathe in through the left; ring finger closes the left, breathe out through the right; in through the right, switch, out through the left. 101.title: The Goddess of bees
101.hook: no creature with two legs or four could kill the demon, so the Goddess came as a swarm of bees; her promise to return
101.carry: the mother comes back, in any form
101.tomorrow: Krishna's conch came from the bottom of the sea. how?
101.howItsDone: Hindus praise the Goddess as Bhramari in hymns, and at Srisailam she is worshipped as Bhramaramba, mother of the bees. In yoga practice, bhramari, the humming bee breath, is done by breathing in through the nose and humming out, often with the ears closed by the thumbs, commonly before meditation.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhringi, and the Lord who is half woman. Your line was Shiva and Shakti can't be split. Today, the Goddess again, and the breath makes a sound.
screen: `SHIVA AND SHAKTI CAN'T BE SPLIT.`

segments.voice: A demon named Aruna wanted to be unbeatable. So he prayed and fasted for years, until the creator god Brahma granted him a boon. In the way it's usually told: no creature with two legs or four could ever kill him. Not gods, not people, not animals. Then he drove the gods out of heaven. They fought, and nothing with two legs or four could touch him. So the Goddess came. Covered in bees.
screen: `A DEMON'S BOON.` → `NOTHING WITH TWO LEGS OR FOUR.` → `SO SHE CAME COVERED IN BEES.`

segments.voice: Bees in her hands, bees in her hair, bees pouring out of her in a dark, humming cloud. Six legs each. The swarm covered Aruna and his army, and that was the end of the unbeatable demon. She's called Bhramari, the Goddess of bees, and she was promised in advance. The Devi Mahatmya, the great poem of the Goddess sung at Navaratri, has her say that when Aruna troubles the worlds, she'll take the form of countless bees, and be praised as Bhramari. A few lines later comes the bigger promise: whenever trouble rises, I will come down and end it. That's the teaching. For many Hindus, God is also Mother, Devi, and she doesn't stay far off. She comes back, again and again, in whatever form the trouble needs, even the smallest. At Srisailam in South India, she's still worshipped as Bhramaramba, mother of the bees. Now the breath that shares her bees' name: bhramari, from bhramara, a bee. Many teachers today keep it simple: a quiet in-breath through the nose, and a long, low hum out, mmm, for as long as the out-breath lasts. Lips closed, teeth slightly apart, jaw loose. To turn it inward, rest your thumbs lightly on the little flaps at the front of your ears and close them. The room disappears, and the hum is all inside. Plenty of people hum when they're scared or can't sleep. A Hindu who knows this story hums knowing who once came as a hum.
screen: `BHRAMARI: THE GODDESS OF BEES.` · `WHENEVER TROUBLE RISES, I WILL COME.` · `GOD AS MOTHER, WHO COMES BACK.` · `BHRAMARA, A BEE: BREATHE IN, HUM OUT.` · then, large: `THE MOTHER COMES BACK, IN ANY FORM.`

segments.voice: Lips gently closed, jaw loose, breathe in through the nose and hum on the out-breath, low and steady, until it runs out; if you like, close the ear flaps with your thumbs and hear the hum inside. Some people offer the hum to the Goddess; it works as plain sound, too, and if you can't make noise where you are, hum silently and feel the lips tingle anyway. After a few rounds, let the humming stop and sit in the quiet it leaves.
Bhramari. From bhramara, the bee. The Goddess who came as a swarm, and the breath that hums like one.

102.title: The conch from the sea
102.hook: Krishna wins back his teacher's drowned son and brings home a conch; why Hindus blow the shankha at worship
102.carry: the conch is breath offered as holy sound
102.tomorrow: the lamp blows out at dinner. what does Arjuna learn?
102.howItsDone: Many Hindu homes and temples blow a conch (shankha) at the start of puja or aarti; the conch is one of the four emblems Vishnu holds. In yoga, ujjayi is breathing through the nose with a slight narrowing of the throat that makes a soft ocean sound, used in seated pranayama and posture practice.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhramari, the Goddess who came as bees. Your line was the mother comes back, in any form. Today, a breath you can hear, and a shell you can blow.
screen: `THE MOTHER COMES BACK, IN ANY FORM.`

segments.voice: When Krishna and his brother Balarama were boys, they went away to study with a teacher named Sandipani, in the city of Avanti. The story says they learned everything he had to teach in sixty-four days. Then came the fee. A student traditionally gives the teacher a gift, guru dakshina, and Sandipani and his wife asked for the one thing no one could give: their son, who had drowned in the sea.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS AT SCHOOL.` → `THE TEACHER'S FEE.` → `A SON LOST AT SEA.`

segments.voice: Krishna went to the shore. The ocean told him a demon named Panchajana, living in the shape of a conch shell, had taken the boy. Krishna went down and fought the demon, and found no boy inside. So he took the demon's shell, went all the way to the city of Yama, the lord of death, and blew it. Yama came out, bowed, and gave the boy back. That shell is Panchajanya, the conch Krishna blew at Kurukshetra, back on day seventy-six. This is from the Bhagavata Purana, and it sits under a sound you can still hear in Hindu homes and temples. The shankha, the conch, is one of the four things Vishnu holds in his hands. At the start of puja or aarti, someone blows a conch: breath turned into a sound that announces God is being welcomed, and, many say, clears the air. That's the teaching: even your breath can be an offering. Krishna's reached the lord of death. Now a breath you can hear without a shell. Ujjayi, usually translated as victorious, from ud, upward, and ji, to win. Teachers explain the name in different ways, and the texts don't settle it. Here's how it's done. Open your mouth and breathe out as if fogging a mirror, haaa. Feel the slight catch in the throat? Close your mouth and keep that catch as you breathe out through the nose, then in. A soft ocean sound, only loud enough for you, the throat relaxed, never squeezed. Think of it as a quiet cousin of the conch.
screen: `PANCHAJANYA: THE CONCH FROM THE SEA.` · `THE SHANKHA, IN VISHNU'S HAND.` · `BLOWN TO BEGIN THE AARTI.` · `UJJAYI: THE VICTORIOUS BREATH.` · then, large: `THE CONCH IS BREATH OFFERED AS HOLY SOUND.`

segments.voice: Open your mouth and breathe out as if fogging a mirror, haaa, then close your mouth and keep that soft catch in the throat as you breathe out and in through the nose. Let it be slow, with the out-breath a little longer, and keep the sound only loud enough for you. Just listen to the waves.
Ujjayi. The victorious breath. A soft ocean sound, made by narrowing the throat just slightly.

screen: `THE CONCH IS BREATH OFFERED AS HOLY SOUND.`

segments.voice: In the Mahabharata, the young princes are learning archery from their teacher Drona, and Arjuna is the keenest of them all. One night he's eating dinner when a gust of wind blows out the lamp. Total dark. And Arjuna notices something. His hand still finds his mouth. Every bite. He doesn't need to see. Years of doing it every day have taught his hand the way.
screen: `A PRINCE AT DINNER.` → `THE LAMP BLOWS OUT.` → `HIS HAND STILL KNOWS THE WAY.`

segments.voice: So Arjuna starts practicing archery at night, in the dark. Drona hears a bowstring twanging after everyone's asleep, goes out, finds him, embraces him, and promises to make him an archer without equal. Later in the same epic, Krishna gives the idea its name. You heard it on day ninety-eight: Arjuna complains that the mind is as restless as the wind, and Krishna says it can still be held, by abhyasa, practice, and by letting go. Abhyasa means steady practice, again and again, over a long time. It's one of Hinduism's most practical teachings: the mind isn't changed in one big moment, but by small repetitions, until it knows the way in the dark. It's why so many Hindus keep a daily practice: a lamp at the shrine, a few minutes of prayer, a few minutes of breath. This week built yours. The word for that breath work is pranayama: prana, breath and life, and ayama, lengthening; some read it as yama, restraint. In the classic picture of yoga it's the fourth of eight steps, after how you treat others, how you live, and how you sit. Here's your five minutes. Watch the breath for thirty seconds. Four in, six out, for a minute. A soft two-count pause, only if it's comfortable. Five rounds of alternate nostrils. Three long hums. A minute of ujjayi, then let it fade, and sit. On a rushed morning, two pieces is still the practice. What matters is coming back.
screen: `ARJUNA PRACTICES IN THE DARK.` · `ABHYASA: PRACTICE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `SMALL REPETITIONS, EVERY DAY.` · `PRANAYAMA: THE FOURTH OF EIGHT STEPS.` · then, large: `ABHYASA IS PRACTICE THAT WORKS IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Here's the short version, to fit the time: watch three breaths just as they are, then four in, six out, three times, then three rounds of alternate nostrils. One long hum, mmm, and then, mouth closed, a few soft ocean breaths. Then let it all go and just sit, the way Arjuna's hand found the way without looking.
Pranayama. Prana, breath and life; ayama, lengthening. The practice of the breath, the fourth step of yoga.

104.title: Mira's groom
104.hook: a little princess is told Krishna is her groom and never forgets; ishta devata, and why people have 'their' mantra
104.carry: one face of god becomes your ishta
104.tomorrow: tied to a stone and thrown into the sea, a saint sang five syllables
104.howItsDone: Many Hindus have an ishta devata, a chosen form of God, and a personal mantra tied to it; in many lineages the mantra is given privately by a guru at initiation (diksha), while others inherit a family deity's mantra or are drawn to one over time. Mirabai's songs to Krishna are still sung in homes and temples.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arjuna in the dark. Your line was abhyasa is practice that works in the dark. Breath week is done. This week adds words to the breath: mantra.
screen: `ABHYASA IS PRACTICE THAT WORKS IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: A little girl in a royal family in Rajasthan watches a wedding procession go past: drums, horses, a groom glittering on his way. She tugs her mother's sleeve. Who's going to be my groom? Her mother, maybe half joking, points to the small image of Krishna in the house. Him. Giridhar Gopal. The little girl believes her, completely. And she never stops.
screen: `A WEDDING GOES BY.` → `WHO WILL MY GROOM BE?` → `HIM. GIRIDHAR GOPAL.`

segments.voice: That girl is Mirabai, the singer you met back on day sixteen. Historians know only a little about her life for sure; this is the story as it's told, and sung. She grew up, was married into a royal family, and kept singing to Krishna anyway. Her best-known line is simple: mere to Giridhar Gopal, dusro na koi. Mine is Giridhar Gopal, no one else. Hinduism has a word for what Mira had. Ishta: desired, cherished, chosen. You met it on day six, in ishta devata, your chosen form of God. Many Hindus speak of one divine reality with many faces: Shiva, Vishnu, Krishna, Rama, the Goddess, Ganesha. The ishta is the face a person is drawn to, and many say it finds you as much as you find it. Choosing one face isn't calling the others wrong: one truth, many names, as day six put it. And a person's mantra usually belongs to their ishta. How does it come? In many lineages a guru gives it in a ceremony called diksha, initiation, and it's kept private. Some families have a family deity, and the mantra comes with the family. And some people, like Mira, are simply drawn, and keep returning. All three are real paths. This week you'll meet four mantras sung openly: for Shiva, for Ganesha, for Krishna, and the Gayatri. You're not being asked to pick a god. You're noticing which sound your heart keeps going back to.
screen: `MINE IS GIRIDHAR GOPAL, NO ONE ELSE.` · `ISHTA — CHOSEN, CHERISHED.` · `ONE TRUTH, MANY FACES.` · `GIVEN, INHERITED, OR FOUND.` · then, large: `ONE FACE OF GOD BECOMES YOUR ISHTA.`

segments.voice: After a few slow breaths from your routine, say softly or silently, on the out-breath, Om three times, then Ram, the name of Rama, three times, then Shanti, peace, three times, noticing how each one sits. You don't have to believe anything to try them; just listen for which one your body wants to say a fourth time. Then say that one, slowly, for the rest of the time.
Ishta. Chosen, cherished. The face of God a person is drawn to, and the mantra that comes with it.

105.title: The stone that floated
105.hook: a Tamil saint tied to a stone sings Shiva's five syllables and floats to shore; the panchakshara as refuge
105.carry: om namah shivaya: shiva's name is a refuge
105.tomorrow: why does Ganesha get the first prayer, even at Shiva's puja?
105.howItsDone: Devotees of Shiva chant Om Namah Shivaya daily, often 108 times on a mala of rudraksha beads, and sing it through the night on Maha Shivaratri; Tamil Shaiva temples still sing Appar's hymns. It is widely chanted openly, though some lineages also give it formally at initiation.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mira and her Giridhar Gopal. Your line was one face of God becomes your ishta. Today, the first of four mantras: Shiva's.
screen: `ONE FACE OF GOD BECOMES YOUR ISHTA.`

segments.voice: South India, more than thirteen hundred years ago. A poet-saint named Appar has angered a king. In the telling, the king tries everything. Appar is shut in a burning kiln, and comes out cool. He's given poison, and it does nothing. An elephant is sent to crush him, and it bows instead. So the king has him tied to a heavy stone and thrown into the sea. Sinking, Appar sings. Shiva's name, verse after verse.
screen: `THE KILN. THE POISON. THE ELEPHANT.` → `TIED TO A STONE.` → `THROWN INTO THE SEA, HE SINGS.`

segments.voice: And the stone floats. It carries him to the shore like a raft. Tamil Shaiva tradition still sings the hymn he sang that day; each verse comes back to the same name: Namasivaya, his true companion. In Sanskrit it's said Om Namah Shivaya. Take off the Om and count what's left: na, mah, shi, vaa, ya. Five syllables, so it's called the panchakshara, the five-syllable mantra. Om is the sound from day two. Namah means I bow. Shivaya, to Shiva, and the name Shiva itself means kind, auspicious. So: Om, I bow to Shiva. Its words go back to a hymn in the Vedas. Here's the teaching under Appar's story. For devotees of Shiva, these five syllables aren't only words about God. Saying the name is itself a refuge, where you go when everything else has failed. Teachers read the syllables many ways. In the Shaiva tradition of the south, they're matched to the five elements: earth, water, fire, air and space. Others hear Shiva's five acts: creating, keeping, dissolving, hiding and revealing. And there's a wordplay people love: namah heard as na mama, not mine. Bowing means you don't have to hold everything up yourself. It's everywhere today: painted on trucks, carved over temple doors, sung all night at Shivaratri, whispered in traffic and in hospital waiting rooms. A bow, and a refuge.
screen: `THE STONE FLOATS.` · `FIVE SYLLABLES: I BOW TO SHIVA.` · `WHERE YOU GO WHEN ALL ELSE FAILS.` · `FIVE ELEMENTS. FIVE ACTS.` · then, large: `OM NAMAH SHIVAYA: SHIVA'S NAME IS A REFUGE.`

segments.voice: Japa means repeating a mantra and counting as you go; twenty-seven is a quarter of a mala, a string of prayer beads, so use beads if you have them, or touch each finger joint with your thumb. On each out-breath, say softly and slowly, Om Namah Shivaya, and if you don't pray, just let it be sound, and count. At twenty-seven, stop, and sit in what's left.
Panchakshara, the five-syllable mantra: na, mah, shi, vaa, ya. Om, I bow to Shiva.
screen: `PANCHAKSHARA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Hold on to it: Om Namah Shivaya, Shiva's name is a refuge. Appar sang it sinking, and floated. See you tomorrow.
